title: Node, npm and Express
blurb: The runtime, the module system, middleware, streams and the npm ecosystem — what a fullstack interview expects you to know about the server side of JavaScript.

questions.q: What does Node give your code that a browser tab does not?
choices: An event loop, so async callbacks can run without blocking the thread
Filesystem, process and raw socket APIs such as fs, child_process and net
Native promises and async/await, which older browsers only get via polyfills
A built-in JSON parser and fetch(), which browsers leave to libraries
questions.why: Both run a JavaScript engine with an event loop, promises, JSON and (since Node 18) fetch. Node adds the OS-facing APIs and drops the DOM, window and localStorage, which is why "window is not defined" shows up during server-side rendering.
questions.asked: A warm-up that checks you know the event loop is shared and the difference is the host APIs.

questions.q: What is the difference between `dependencies` and `devDependencies`?
choices: devDependencies are installed globally; dependencies go in the local node_modules
dependencies are pinned by the lockfile; devDependencies float within their range
dependencies are needed at runtime; devDependencies only to build, lint and test
devDependencies are bundled into the build output; dependencies load at runtime
questions.why: `npm ci --omit=dev` in a production image skips devDependencies, giving a smaller, less exposed container. Both kinds are local and both are locked by package-lock.json. Putting TypeScript or a test runner in dependencies is a common slip.
questions.asked: Checks you have built a production image rather than only run `npm install` on a laptop.

questions.q: What does a committed `package-lock.json` guarantee?
choices: That every package in the tree has passed npm's malware and audit checks
That npm install always fetches the newest version each range allows
Only faster installs, because npm can skip downloading the tarballs
The exact resolved version and integrity hash of every package in the tree
questions.why: Without a lockfile, `^1.2.0` can resolve to a different 1.x on the CI machine than on yours. The lockfile says nothing about safety: a locked version can still be malicious. Use `npm ci` in CI; it installs strictly from the lockfile and fails if package.json disagrees.
questions.asked: Follow-up: "what is the difference between npm install and npm ci?"

questions.q: Which versions does the range `^1.2.3` allow?
choices: Only patch releases of 1.2, from 1.2.3 up to but excluding 1.3.0
Any release at or above 1.2.3, including 2.x and later majors
Any 1.x.y at or above 1.2.3: new minors and patches, never 2.0.0
Exactly 1.2.3, unless npm update is run with the --latest flag
questions.why: The caret allows anything that does not change the leftmost non-zero part; `~1.2.3` is the patch-only range. Semver's promise that minors are compatible holds often enough to be useful and not always enough to skip the lockfile. Note `^0.2.3` allows only 0.2.x.
questions.asked: Leads to "so why did a minor update break production?" and the lockfile.

questions.q: What is Express middleware?
choices: A plugin registered once at startup that Express calls for each route file
A wrapper Express puts around database calls to manage their connections
A hook that runs after the response is sent, for logging and cleanup
A (req, res, next) function in an ordered chain that handles or passes on
questions.why: Order is everything: a body parser registered after a route means `req.body` is undefined there, and an auth middleware registered after a route does not protect it. Middleware can run code after the response too, but that is one use, not the definition.
questions.asked: The follow-up is always "what happens if you register it after the routes?"

questions.q: Why does this error handler never run?
choices: Error handlers take three parameters, so the extra err makes Express skip it
It must call next(err) itself, or Express treats the error as unhandled
It is registered before the route, so errors thrown there never reach it
res.status() is not available inside error handlers, so the call throws
questions.why: Express walks the stack in registration order, and an error only travels forward to error handlers registered after the point where it happened. Error handlers are recognised by having four parameters; dropping `next` turns one into ordinary middleware.
questions.asked: A code-review classic; the four-parameter rule is the follow-up.

questions.q: In Express 4, why does a rejected promise in an async route handler not reach the error handler?
choices: Express 4 ignores the returned promise, so you must catch and call next(err)
The error handler must itself be declared async to receive rejected promises
Express 4 forwards rejections only when the value is an instance of Error
Express 4 rejects async functions as route handlers when routes are registered
questions.why: Express 4 calls the handler and discards what it returns, so the rejection is unhandled: since Node 15 that crashes the process by default (`--unhandled-rejections=throw`), and if an `unhandledRejection` handler is registered the request hangs until the client times out instead. Wrap handlers in a helper that attaches `.catch(next)`, or move to Express 5, which forwards rejected promises to the error handler.
questions.asked: A very practical Express question: this bug produces either a crashed process or mysterious hanging requests, depending on how unhandled rejections are configured.

questions.q: In Node 24, how do CommonJS and ES modules differ?
choices: require loads synchronously at run time; import is statically analysed and hoisted
ESM is browser-only syntax, so Node rewrites every import into a require call
CommonJS was removed in Node 22, so require only works behind a runtime flag
Nothing that matters: each loads the other freely, with no caveats whatsoever
questions.why: Static imports enable tree shaking and top-level await. Node picks the loader by extension, the package "type" field, or (since 22.7) syntax detection. `require()` of an ES module works unflagged since 22.12, but not for a graph with top-level await, so interop still has a caveat. In ESM, `__dirname` is `import.meta.dirname`.
questions.asked: Checks your module knowledge is current: older answers say ESM needs "type": "module" and require(esm) is impossible.

questions.q: Why stream a large file to the client rather than read it into memory first?
choices: Streams are always faster, because they bypass the kernel's page cache
fs.readFile refuses any file over 100 MB, so a stream is the only option
A stream moves the file in chunks, so memory stays flat per request
Streams gzip the data on the fly, so less of it crosses the network
questions.why: Ten concurrent requests each buffering a 500 MB file is 5 GB of RAM and an OOM kill. Streams also start sending immediately, so time to first byte improves. They are not inherently faster in throughput, and `readFile` only fails near 2 GiB.
questions.asked: Checks you think about memory per request, not per process, once concurrency is involved.

questions.q: What is backpressure in a Node stream?
choices: The consumer signalling it is full, so the producer pauses until it drains
An error in the destination travelling back upstream to close the source
The internal buffer spilling over to disk once it grows past highWaterMark
The retry a writable stream performs when a write to the socket fails
questions.why: When `write()` returns false the producer should wait for `drain`. Ignore it and you buffer a fast source in memory while a slow destination crawls. `pipeline()` handles backpressure and error propagation for you; hand-rolled `on('data')` loops usually do not.
questions.asked: Separates people who have piped a real upload or export from people who have read about streams.

questions.q: How should configuration reach a Node service in production?
choices: A config.json per environment, committed and selected by NODE_ENV
Constants per environment, compiled into the build by the bundler
Command-line flags only, so the running config is visible in ps
Environment variables validated at startup, secrets from a store
questions.why: Environment config is the twelve-factor default and what containers and CI expect. Validate at boot and crash loudly: discovering a missing DATABASE_URL on the first request at 3am is much worse than at deploy. Flags in `ps` leak secrets to anyone on the host.
questions.asked: Tests whether one build artefact can move unchanged through every environment.

questions.q: What happens by default when an exception is never caught in Node?
choices: Node logs the stack trace and carries on with the next queued event
The process exits with an error, and a supervisor should restart it
Express's error middleware catches it and returns a 500 to the client
The event loop restarts, dropping pending callbacks but keeping state
questions.why: After an uncaught exception the application state is unknown, so log, flush and exit, and let the orchestrator start a clean process. Express only catches what is thrown synchronously in its handlers (and, in Express 5, rejected promises); a throw inside a timer or event callback escapes it.
questions.asked: The follow-up is whether keeping the process alive with an uncaughtException handler is a good idea (it is not).

questions.q: How do you use more than one CPU core with a Node web service?
choices: Nothing to do: libuv spreads your JavaScript across every core itself
Raise UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE so more of your JavaScript runs in parallel
Run several processes (cluster or containers); worker_threads for CPU work
Convert handlers to async/await so each request gets its own OS thread
questions.why: JavaScript executes on one thread per process. The libuv pool runs some native I/O and crypto work, not your code, so resizing it does not parallelise handlers. Most services scale by running N containers behind a load balancer, which also gives restarts and rolling deploys.
questions.asked: Checks you know the single-threaded model and how production actually scales it.

questions.q: What blocks the Node event loop?
choices: Synchronous CPU work or sync I/O such as fs.readFileSync in a handler
Every await, because the whole process pauses until the promise settles
Database queries, because the driver waits for the network reply
Large responses, because res.send waits for the client to download
questions.why: Async I/O is handed to the OS or the libuv pool, and the loop serves other requests meanwhile; `await` suspends only the current function. A single two-second JSON.parse of a huge payload stalls every concurrent request on that process.
questions.asked: Then: "so how would you handle a CPU-heavy endpoint?" A worker thread, a queue, or a different runtime.

questions.q: What is the difference between a liveness check and a readiness check?
choices: Liveness checks the database is reachable; readiness checks the port is open
Liveness runs once at startup; readiness runs again on every incoming request
They are the same probe, except readiness also reports the deployed version
Liveness asks whether to restart the process; readiness whether to send it traffic
questions.why: A failed liveness check means "this process is wedged, restart it"; a failed readiness check means "do not route to me right now" (warming up, dependency down). Putting a database check in liveness means a brief database blip restarts every instance at once.
questions.asked: Checks you have seen a restart storm, or can reason about one.

questions.q: Where should request validation happen in an Express API?
choices: In database constraints only, since they are the final authority
In the frontend form, since that is where users enter the data
At the boundary, before the handler's logic or any database call
Wherever each value is first used, deep in the service layer
questions.why: Validate once at the boundary and the rest of the code can trust its inputs. Constraints are a last line of defence with poor error messages, and client-side validation is a UX feature: anyone can post directly to your API.
questions.asked: Checks you treat the client as untrusted and know where the trust boundary is.

questions.q: What is the risk of a transitive dependency you never chose?
choices: None, provided the direct dependency comes from a trusted publisher
It only lengthens install time, since unused code is never loaded
A compromised deep package runs with your process's full privileges
npm refuses packages not listed directly in your package.json
questions.why: Install scripts and runtime code both execute as your process, with its network, filesystem and secrets. Mitigations: pin with a lockfile, audit in CI, prefer fewer well-maintained dependencies, and consider `--ignore-scripts`.
questions.asked: Supply-chain incidents are now a routine interview topic; the lockfile and install scripts are the follow-ups.

questions.q: In Express, what does `res.json(data)` do that `res.send(JSON.stringify(data))` does not?
choices: It streams the body in chunks instead of buffering the whole string
It skips building the string first, so it serialises noticeably faster
Nothing: both send the same bytes with the same response headers
It sets Content-Type to application/json and applies the app's JSON settings
questions.why: `res.send` with a string sets `Content-Type: text/html`, so clients that branch on the header treat the body as text. `res.json` sets the JSON type and honours the `json replacer` and `json spaces` settings. It still builds the whole string in memory.
questions.asked: Small, but it is the cause of "the response is a string" bugs on the client.

questions.q: What does graceful shutdown mean for a Node web service?
choices: Restarting the process automatically whenever it exits with an error
Flushing buffered logs in an uncaughtException handler just before exiting
Closing the database pool first, so that no new queries can start
On SIGTERM: stop accepting, finish in-flight requests, close pools, exit
questions.why: During a rolling deploy the orchestrator sends SIGTERM and waits. Exiting immediately drops requests mid-flight; closing the pool first makes the in-flight requests fail instead. `server.close()` stops new connections and calls back when the existing ones finish.
questions.asked: A strong signal for anyone claiming deployment experience.

questions.q: How should a production Node service write its logs?
choices: console.log lines to a file that the app itself rotates each day
Errors only, because info-level logs cost too much to ship and store
Full request and response bodies, so that any bug can be replayed
Structured JSON to stdout, with levels and a request correlation id
questions.why: Containers collect stdout, so the app should not manage files, and structured logs are queryable. Info logs are what reconstruct a request; bodies leak passwords, tokens and card numbers.
questions.asked: Leads to what you must never log, and how you find one request across services.

questions.q: In Express 5, what does `app.use(express.json())` do with an incoming request?
choices: Parses every request body as JSON, whatever its Content-Type header says
Parses bodies with a JSON Content-Type into req.body, up to 100kb by default
Validates JSON bodies against the route's schema and rejects bad ones with 400
Parses JSON bodies of any size, and serialises every res.send() as JSON too
questions.why: It only acts when the Content-Type matches application/json; otherwise `req.body` stays undefined in Express 5 (Express 4 set it to `{}`). Bodies over the 100kb default are rejected with 413 and malformed JSON with 400. Raise the limit on the routes that need it rather than globally.
questions.asked: Checks you know the parser is conditional and bounded, which explains both "req.body is undefined" and "413" tickets.

questions.q: Why is `path.join(baseDir, req.query.file)` dangerous in a download route?
choices: path.join is synchronous, so it blocks the event loop on each request
Input such as ../../etc/passwd resolves outside the intended folder
path.join follows symlinks, so it can reach any file on the disk
path.join does not normalise separators, so Windows paths break
questions.why: `path.join` resolves `..` segments, so it happily walks out of `baseDir`. Resolve the path, then check it still starts with the base directory, or map input to an allowlist of names. It is a pure string operation: fast, and it never touches the filesystem.
questions.asked: Path traversal is the Node-specific injection interviewers expect you to spot in review.

questions.q: What does `express.Router()` give you in a growing Express app?
choices: A separate HTTP server per feature, each listening on its own port
Routes generated automatically from the files in a routes/ folder
A mini-app with its own routes and middleware, mounted at a path prefix
A registry that loads each route file lazily on its first request
questions.why: `app.use('/orders', ordersRouter)` mounts a router so its paths are relative to the prefix, and middleware added to that router (auth, validation) applies only to its routes. Express has no file-based routing; that is a feature of other frameworks.
questions.asked: Checks you can structure a codebase past one index.js.

questions.q: A client requests `GET /users/42?tab=orders`. What does this handler see?
choices: req.params.id is '42' and req.query.tab is 'orders'
req.params.id is 42 and req.query.tab is 'orders'
req.query.id is '42' and req.params.tab is 'orders'
req.body.id is '42' and req.query.tab is 'orders'
questions.why: Path segments named in the route land in `req.params`, the query string in `req.query`, and `req.body` is only filled by a body parser. Everything from the URL is a string, so `42` must be parsed and validated before it is used as a number.
questions.asked: A junior screen favourite; the string-not-number detail is what the interviewer is listening for.

questions.q: Your build emits hashed filenames such as `app.3f9a.js`. How should `express.static` cache them?
choices: With no-store, so users can never run an outdated JavaScript bundle
With a long max-age and immutable, since a changed file gets a new name
With no Cache-Control header at all, so each browser picks a sensible default
With max-age=0 on the assets and a long max-age on index.html itself
questions.why: A content hash means the URL changes whenever the bytes do, so a year-long `max-age` with `immutable` is safe. `express.static` defaults to `max-age=0` with an ETag, so every load revalidates. Keep index.html revalidated (the reverse of the last option), or users never see the new hashes.
questions.asked: Checks you connect bundler output to HTTP caching, which is where "users see the old version" tickets come from.

questions.q: What does adding the `helmet` middleware to an Express app do?
choices: Validates and sanitises request bodies against injection attacks
Rate-limits each client IP to stop brute force and denial of service
Encrypts cookies and session data with a key from the environment
Sets security response headers such as CSP, HSTS and nosniff
questions.why: Helmet sets headers like Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security and X-Content-Type-Options, and removes X-Powered-By. It does nothing to requests: validation, rate limiting and cookie signing are separate middleware.
questions.asked: Checks you know what a common dependency actually does rather than treating it as "security, done".

questions.q: Why does `express-session` with its default store break once you run three instances behind a load balancer?
choices: The default MemoryStore lives in one process, so the others lack the session
The cookie is signed per instance, so the other two reject its signature
Each session holds a row lock in the database, so the instances deadlock
Sessions are tied to one TCP connection, which the balancer does not reuse
questions.why: Each process has its own MemoryStore, so a request that lands on another instance looks logged out. The docs also warn MemoryStore leaks and is not for production. Use a shared store such as Redis or the database; sticky sessions only hide the problem until an instance restarts.
questions.asked: A direct test of whether you have scaled a stateful Express app past one instance.

questions.q: Requests for a missing order log 'Cannot set headers after they are sent'. Why?
choices: db.find resolved after Express had already sent a default response
res.status() sends the headers at once, before json() can add its own
The 404 branch has no return, so res.json(order) also runs after it
Async handlers must call next() after responding, or Express resends
questions.why: The 404 is sent, execution falls through, and the second `res.json` tries to set headers on a finished response. Write `return res.status(404).json(...)`. `res.status()` only sets the code; nothing is sent until `json()` or `send()`.
questions.asked: One of the most common Express errors in real logs; spotting the missing return in review is the skill.

questions.q: Behind a load balancer, `req.ip` is always the balancer's address and `req.secure` is false. What is the Express fix?
choices: Read `req.headers['x-forwarded-for']` in each handler yourself and take its first entry as the client
Set `app.set('trust proxy', 1)`, so Express reads X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto
Enable `app.enable('https')` so Express knows the client connection was TLS-terminated upstream
Mount the app on `https.createServer` with the balancer's certificate, so req.secure becomes true
questions.why: Express only honours the X-Forwarded-* headers when `trust proxy` says which hops to believe; `1` trusts the nearest proxy, after which `req.ip`, `req.ips`, `req.protocol` and `req.secure` describe the original client. Reading the header yourself lets any client forge its IP, which breaks rate limiting and audit logs; trusting every hop (`true`) has the same flaw if the app is reachable directly. There is no `https` setting, and the app's own TLS is irrelevant because the balancer terminated it.
questions.asked: The Express version of the forwarded-headers question; wrong values break secure cookies, redirects and per-IP rate limits.
